title: A tale of two isotopes: Spatial variation in HCN fractionation toward young cores
summary: Context. Isotopic fractionation can serve as a powerful tracer of the chemical evolution during star and planet formation. To accurately interpret observations, it is crucial to identify the dominant pathways of nitrogen and carbon fractionation at different evolutionary stages. Aims. We aim to study nitrogen and carbon fractionation in a sample of young cores at the onset of star formation. Methods. We map H$^{13}$CN and HC$^{15}$N around one starless and three pre-stellar cores. We compute the $N$(H$^{13}$CN)/$N$(HC$^{15}$N) column density ratio across the cores and compare the distribution with $N$(H$_2$) maps from $\textit{Herschel}$/SPIRE. In addition, we calculate $^{14}$N/$^{15}$N maps using the double isotope method for comparison with earlier studies. The results are compared with astrochemical modeling of carbon and nitrogen fractionation for a one-dimensional pre-stellar core model. Results. The computed $N$(H$^{13}$CN)/$N$(HC$^{15}$N) ratio exhibit clear spatial variation across the maps. This variation is correlated with $N$(H$_2$) in three out of four cores. Conclusions. Our analysis reveals a correlation between the H$^{13}$CN/HC$^{15}$N ratios and the $N$(H$_2$) maps. According to the astrochemical model, the correlation is mainly due to variations in the $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratio. Consequently, the results caution against applying the double-isotope method to derive $^{14}$N/$^{15}$N ratios without independently assessing possible spatial variations in the $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratio. Furthermore, the leading cause of the isotopic variation in the model is not isotope-selective photodissociation, but rather more efficient fractionation through exchange reactions at lower temperatures in the denser regions of the cores.

AI.tldr: This study maps H¹³CN and HC¹⁵N in one starless and three pre-stellar cores, finding spatial variations in the H¹³CN/HC¹⁵N ratio correlated with H₂ column density. Astrochemical modeling reveals this correlation is primarily driven by variations in the ¹²C/¹³C ratio rather than isotope-selective photodissociation, cautioning against the double-isotope method for deriving ¹⁴N/¹⁵N ratios without accounting for ¹²C/¹³C spatial variations. The dominant fractionation mechanism is exchange reactions at low temperatures in dense regions.
AI.motivation: To identify the dominant pathways of nitrogen and carbon isotopic fractionation at different evolutionary stages of star formation, using isotopic ratios as tracers of chemical evolution.
AI.method: Mapping H¹³CN and HC¹⁵N around one starless and three pre-stellar cores; computing N(H¹³CN)/N(HC¹⁵N) column density ratios; comparing with Herschel/SPIRE H₂ maps; calculating ¹⁴N/¹⁵N maps via the double isotope method; comparing results with 1D astrochemical modeling of carbon and nitrogen fractionation.
AI.result: The N(H¹³CN)/N(HC¹⁵N) ratio shows clear spatial variation correlated with N(H₂) in three out of four cores. The astrochemical model indicates this correlation is mainly due to variations in the ¹²C/¹³C ratio.
AI.conclusion: The correlation between H¹³CN/HC¹⁵N ratios and H₂ column density cautions against using the double-isotope method for ¹⁴N/¹⁵N without assessing ¹²C/¹³C spatial variations. The primary driver of isotopic variation is exchange reactions at low temperatures in dense regions, not isotope-selective photodissociation.

title: An interstellar energetic and non-aqueous pathway to peptide formation
summary: The origin of the molecular building blocks of life is a central question in science. A few $α$-amino acids such as glycine, the simplest proteinogenic amino acid, have been detected in meteorites and comets, indicating an extraterrestrial origin for some prebiotic molecules. However, the formation of peptides, short chains of $α$-amino acids linked by peptide bonds, under astrophysical conditions has remained unresolved. Here we show that the building blocks of proteins can form in interstellar ice analogues exposed to ionising radiation, without the presence of liquid water. Using isotopically labelled glycine irradiated with protons at cryogenic temperatures, we detect the formation of glycylglycine, the simplest dipeptide, along with deuterated and non-deuterated water as by-products. Peptide bond formation is confirmed by infrared spectroscopy and high-resolution mass spectrometry, which also reveal the production of other complex organic species. These findings demonstrate a non-aqueous route to peptide formation under space-like conditions and suggest that such molecules could form in the cold interstellar medium and be incorporated into forming planetary systems. Our results challenge aqueous-centric models of early biochemical evolution and broaden potential settings for the origins of life.

AI.tldr: Peptide bond formation (glycylglycine) can occur in interstellar ice analogues under ionising radiation at cryogenic temperatures without liquid water, challenging aqueous-centric models of life's origins.
AI.motivation: While some α-amino acids have been detected in meteorites and comets, the formation of peptides (chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds) under astrophysical conditions has remained unresolved.
AI.method: Isotopically labelled glycine was irradiated with protons at cryogenic temperatures in interstellar ice analogues. Products were analyzed using infrared spectroscopy and high-resolution mass spectrometry.
AI.result: Formation of glycylglycine (simplest dipeptide) was detected, along with deuterated and non-deuterated water as by-products. Other complex organic species were also produced.
AI.conclusion: A non-aqueous route to peptide formation exists under space-like conditions, suggesting such molecules could form in cold interstellar medium and be incorporated into forming planetary systems, challenging aqueous-centric models of early biochemical evolution.

title: Constraining the shape of dark matter haloes using only starlight II. Tests of the technique with objects of known gravitational potential
summary: Under the collisionless cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm, galaxies with stellar masses below 10**(5-6) Msun are expected to preserve primordial cuspy dark matter (DM) profiles. Because baryonic feedback should be too weak to transform cusps into cores at these masses, such galaxies provide especially sensitive tests of DM physics. If cores are observed in these systems, they could indicate departures from CDM. To address this problem, Sanchez Almeida et al. (2025) introduced the Eddington Inversion Method tool (EIM-tool), a photometry-based diagnostic that avoids the need for long-term spectroscopic observations and is suitable for the analysis of the forthcoming large photometric surveys of galaxies. The method relies on the fact that embedding a stellar distribution with a central core inside a cuspy NFW halo can require a negative phase-space distribution function f, which is physically impossible. By fitting observed stellar surface densities using f as a free parameter, EIM-tool tests whether an assumed gravitational potential is physically consistent with an observed stellar distribution. This paper validates EIM-tool using globular clusters, dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs), and numerical simulations with independently known potentials. Applied to 21 globular clusters, the method rejected NFW cusps in 71\% of cases while consistently favoring cored Schuster-Plummer models, accurately recovering expected core radii. Applied to dSphs, EIM-tool reproduced conclusions from classical dynamical studies: Sculptor and Fornax favored cored halos, whereas Draco remained compatible with a cusp. Tests on EDGE and FIRE simulations further showed that the tool reliably rejects cuspy NFW profiles when the true DM distribution is core-like. Overall, these results establish EIM-tool as a robust and efficient photometric method for distinguishing cored and cuspy DM halos.

AI.tldr: The paper validates the Eddington Inversion Method tool (EIM-tool), a photometric diagnostic that distinguishes cored vs. cuspy dark matter halos in low-mass galaxies without requiring spectroscopy. Tests on globular clusters, dwarf spheroidal galaxies, and simulations show it reliably rejects cuspy NFW profiles when the true DM distribution is core-like, establishing it as a robust method for DM physics tests.
AI.motivation: Under CDM, galaxies with stellar masses below 10^(5-6) Msun should retain primordial cuspy DM profiles since baryonic feedback is too weak to transform cusps into cores. If cores are observed in these systems, it could indicate departures from CDM, providing sensitive tests of DM physics. However, traditional methods require long-term spectroscopic observations, motivating the need for a photometry-based diagnostic suitable for large photometric surveys.
AI.method: EIM-tool uses the Eddington Inversion Method to test whether an assumed gravitational potential (e.g., NFW cusp or cored Schuster-Plummer) is physically consistent with an observed stellar surface density. It relies on the principle that embedding a cored stellar distribution in a cuspy NFW halo can produce a negative phase-space distribution function f, which is physically impossible. The tool fits observed stellar surface densities using f as a free parameter to determine consistency.
AI.result: Applied to 21 globular clusters, EIM-tool rejected NFW cusps in 71% of cases and consistently favored cored Schuster-Plummer models, accurately recovering expected core radii. For dSphs, it reproduced classical dynamical results: Sculptor and Fornax favored cored halos, while Draco remained compatible with a cusp. Tests on EDGE and FIRE simulations showed the tool reliably rejects cuspy NFW profiles when the true DM distribution is core-like.
AI.conclusion: EIM-tool is established as a robust and efficient photometric method for distinguishing cored and cuspy DM halos, enabling tests of CDM predictions in the low-mass galaxy regime without requiring expensive spectroscopic observations.

title: eROSITA all-sky survey - stars and optical loading
comment: Paper submitted to Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: eROSITA (extended ROentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array) on board the Spectrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) spacecraft has performed the eROSITA All-Sky Survey (eRASS) at X-ray energies. We study the brighter stars to assess the impact of optical loading in the eROSITA all-sky survey, here specifically the eRASS:3. Further we use thermal plasma models to investigate the general properties of stellar eRASS sources and compare optical loading affected stars to coronal sources. We compare data from Gaia DR3, Tycho-2, 2MASS and the SIMBAD database with the eRASS count rates of brighter stars. We analyze X-ray images, light curves and spectra for sources suspected to be affected by optical loading and determine their properties. eROSITA source properties are checked in comparison to genuine coronal sources with generated sets of APEC model spectra, where we determine rate conversion factors and hardness ratios for stellar X-ray emitter. Regarding optical loading we find a clear correlation between optical brightness and observed minimum count rate in the range of about 2\,--\,5 mag (V/G band), which then saturates for very bright sources. While magnitude and color are the main determinants, exposure depth and specific scanning paths also matter. For intrinsic X-ray emitters, optical contamination is likewise observed. We characterize the fake X-ray sources, address pseudo variability and spectral properties. To interpret stellar eRASS data, hardness ratios and count rate conversions for thermal plasma models are provided. The eROSITA data is prone to optical loading, which was studied in greater detail. The optical loading flag for the DR2 is set, if sources are brighter than 5.0~mag (B, V, G) or 3.5~mag (J). It is somewhat dependent on exposure depth, but we expect only minor changes for future data releases.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes optical loading in eROSITA All-Sky Survey (eRASS:3) data, showing a correlation between optical brightness (2-5 mag) and observed minimum X-ray count rates, with saturation for very bright sources. The study characterizes fake X-ray sources from optical contamination, provides hardness ratios and count rate conversions for stellar coronal sources, and establishes the optical loading flag threshold (B/V/G > 5.0 mag, J > 3.5 mag) used for DR2.
AI.motivation: To assess the impact of optical loading on eROSITA all-sky survey X-ray observations of bright stars, and to distinguish optically contaminated sources from genuine coronal X-ray emitters.
AI.method: Comparison of Gaia DR3, Tycho-2, 2MASS, and SIMBAD data with eRASS count rates; X-ray image, light curve, and spectral analysis; generation of APEC model spectra for genuine coronal sources to determine rate conversion factors and hardness ratios; correlation analysis between optical magnitude and minimum X-ray count rates.
AI.result: Clear correlation between optical brightness (2-5 mag) and observed minimum count rate, saturating for very bright sources. Optical contamination also affects intrinsic X-ray emitters. Fake X-ray sources show pseudo variability and altered spectral properties. Optical loading flag set at >5.0 mag (B,V,G) or >3.5 mag (J) for DR2.
AI.conclusion: eROSITA data is prone to optical loading; the established flag thresholds are somewhat dependent on exposure depth but expected to remain largely unchanged for future data releases. Hardness ratios and count rate conversions for thermal plasma models are provided to aid interpretation of stellar eRASS data.

title: J-ATLAS: Javalambre Andromeda and Triangulum Legacy Astrophysical Survey
comment: The Hidden Beauty of the Galactic Outskirts. Proceeding IAU Symposium 403, 2025
summary: The outskirts of nearby galaxies preserve long-lived signatures of hierarchical assembly and provide a fossil record of galaxy formation. J-ATLAS, the Javalambre Andromeda and Triangulum Legacy Astrophysical Survey, is a proposed wide-field optical photospectroscopic survey of the M31--M33 system with JST/T250 and JPCam. Using the dense J-PAS filter system, it will deliver homogeneous low-resolution optical SEDs for resolved stars, compact stellar systems, emission-line sources, and background objects across the nearest massive spiral-galaxy environment visible from the northern sky. The survey will map disks, halos, streams, satellites, and the intergalactic region, constraining stellar populations, photometric metallicities, carbon-rich evolved stars, star clusters, planetary nebulae, and low-surface-brightness substructure. We also present the ongoing pilot survey, centred on the Giant Southern Stream and Andromeda~I, whose 92 complete pointings are being analysed to validate crowded-field photometry, calibration, source classification, and photometric metallicity diagnostics before extending the methodology to the full J-ATLAS footprint survey.

AI.tldr: J-ATLAS is a proposed wide-field optical photospectroscopic survey of the M31-M33 system using JST/T250 and JPCam, designed to map resolved stars, stellar populations, and substructures in the nearest massive spiral galaxy environment. A pilot survey centered on the Giant Southern Stream and Andromeda I is underway to validate photometry and calibration methods.
AI.motivation: To study hierarchical assembly and galaxy formation using the fossil record preserved in the outskirts of nearby galaxies, specifically the M31-M33 system.
AI.method: J-ATLAS will use the JST/T250 telescope and JPCam with the dense J-PAS filter system to obtain homogeneous low-resolution optical SEDs for resolved stars, compact stellar systems, emission-line sources, and background objects. A pilot survey with 92 complete pointings is being conducted to validate crowd-field photometry, calibration, source classification, and photometric metallicity diagnostics.
AI.result: The pilot survey is ongoing; results will inform extension of the methodology to the full J-ATLAS footprint.
AI.conclusion: J-ATLAS will provide constraints on stellar populations, photometric metallicities, carbon-rich evolved stars, star clusters, planetary nebulae, and low-surface-brightness substructure across the M31-M33 system, offering a comprehensive fossil record of galaxy formation.

title: Evolutionary variations of superficial iron and calcium abundance in main sequence A stars
comment: 12 pages, 12 figures, accepted to Astronomy Letters
summary: Main sequence stellar evolution models were computed together with solution of the equations of atomic diffusion for 16 elements from hydrogen to nickel. The grid of evolutionary tracks comprises the models with stellar masses ranged from 1.4 to $2.5M_\odot$ computed for initial helium and metal abundances $Y=0.28$ and $Z=0.02$, respectively. The calculations were done for the mass loss rates $10^{-15}M_\odot/\textrm{yr}\le\dot M\le 10^{-12}M_\odot/\textrm{yr}$ as well as for $\dot M=0$. The high superficial abundance of iron in Am stars is shown to be due to the radiative acceleration acting on the atoms of iron. The significantly smaller absorption coefficient of calcium is responsible for its gravitational settling and accumulation above its opacity maximum at $T\sim 10^6\:\textrm{K}$. Recover of the superficial calcium abundance is due to plunge of the outer convection zone bottom to layers with its excessive abundance. A significant role in the evolutionary variations of superficial abundances of chemical elements belongs to the intermediate convection zone arising for the first $\lesssim 300$ Myr due to accumulation of the atoms of iron and nickel in the layers with temperature $T\sim 2\times 10^5\:\textrm{K}$. In stars with mass $M\le 1.9M_\odot$ both the outer and intermediate convection zones merge due to evolutionary descend of the bottom of the outer convection zone so that overabundant iron and nickel are transported to the outer layers by convection. The merging of the convective zones is responsible for considerable variations of superficial abundances of calcium and iron with duration ranging from a quarter to a half of the main--sequence lifetime depending on the stellar mass. Therefore, Am stars as well as slowly rotating nonmagnetic A main--sequence stars have the common origin, whereas appearance of their chemical anomalies depend of the stellar mass and age.

AI.tldr: This paper models main sequence stellar evolution with atomic diffusion for 16 elements in stars of 1.4–2.5 M⊙, showing that Am star chemical anomalies (iron overabundance, calcium depletion) arise from radiative acceleration, gravitational settling, and convection zone interactions varying with mass and age.
AI.motivation: To understand the origin of chemical peculiarities in Am (metallic-line) stars by modeling atomic diffusion, radiative acceleration, and convective mixing in main sequence A-type stars.
AI.method: Stellar evolution models with atomic diffusion equations for 16 elements (H–Ni), computed for masses 1.4–2.5 M⊙, with Y=0.28, Z=0.02, and mass loss rates 0 to 10⁻¹² M⊙/yr.
AI.result: Iron overabundance in Am stars is due to radiative acceleration; calcium depletion results from gravitational settling below its opacity maximum. An intermediate convection zone forms (≲300 Myr) from iron/nickel accumulation at T∼2×10⁵ K. In M≤1.9 M⊙, this zone merges with the outer convection zone, transporting excess iron/nickel to the surface, causing variable abundance patterns lasting 25–50% of the main-sequence lifetime.
AI.conclusion: Am stars and slowly rotating nonmagnetic A stars share a common origin; their chemical anomalies depend on stellar mass and age rather than a fundamentally different formation mechanism.

title: The Stellar Winds Atlas II: Black Hole Formation at Solar Metallicity
comment: Submitted to Open Journal of Astrophysics. Comments welcome
summary: Stellar winds are a primary source of uncertainty in predicting the masses of black holes (BHs) from massive stars. At solar metallicity, theoretical models lead to widely divergent results due to differing wind prescriptions. A key obstacle remains the lack of systematic investigations across a common parameter space. To address this, we construct a ``Wind Atlas'' using detailed 1D MESA stellar evolution models and population synthesis techniques to estimate the Galactic population of solar metallicity BH progenitors. We systematically investigate 14 distinct wind models, ranging from the most traditional and widespread prescriptions to the most recent. By evaluating stellar evolution across this extensive grid, we show that the final BH mass is dictated by a fundamental bifurcation: whether a star collapses as a cool supergiant or is first stripped of its envelope to become a Wolf-Rayet (WR) star. If a star enters the WR stage, its strong thick winds dominate, making the final mass sensitive to the WR wind prescription while largely erasing the memory of its prior mass-loss history. Conversely, stars that face core collapse as supergiants form significantly more massive BHs, producing a mass peak around an initial mass of 40 $M_\odot$. Rather than simply reproducing these divergent outcomes, our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that this bifurcation is universally controlled by the highly uncertain mass loss during the cool supergiant phase. This framework strongly constrains the problem of BH mass prediction by identifying two key bottlenecks for future studies: envelope stripping efficiency and WR mass-loss rates. Our atlas provides a clear baseline for interpreting current theoretical discrepancies and testing wind models against observational constraints, such as the Galactic WR/OB population ratio.

AI.tldr: This study constructs a "Wind Atlas" using MESA stellar evolution models to systematically evaluate 14 different wind prescriptions for solar-metallicity black hole progenitors. It reveals a fundamental bifurcation: stars that become Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars produce smaller BHs due to strong WR winds, while stars collapsing as cool supergiants form more massive BHs (peak ~40 M☉). The key uncertainty is mass loss during the cool supergiant phase, which controls envelope stripping and determines which path a star follows.
AI.motivation: Stellar wind prescriptions introduce major uncertainties in predicting black hole masses from massive stars, and theoretical models diverge widely due to the lack of systematic investigations across a common parameter space. This study aims to address this gap.
AI.method: The authors used 1D MESA stellar evolution models combined with population synthesis techniques to construct a "Wind Atlas," systematically investigating 14 distinct wind models across a common parameter space of solar-metallicity BH progenitors.
AI.result: Final BH mass is governed by a bifurcation: (1) stars stripped to become WR stars experience strong thick winds that dominate mass loss, erasing prior mass-loss history and yielding smaller BHs; (2) stars collapsing as cool supergiants form significantly more massive BHs with a peak around 40 M☉. The bifurcation is universally controlled by mass loss during the cool supergiant phase.
AI.conclusion: The framework identifies two key bottlenecks for future BH mass prediction: envelope stripping efficiency and WR mass-loss rates. The Wind Atlas provides a baseline for interpreting theoretical discrepancies and testing wind models against observations like the Galactic WR/OB population ratio.

title: Constraints from parallaxes and average period spacings in the asteroseismic study of 8 DAVs
comment: 23 pages, 18 figures, published in the Astrophysical Journal
summary: With space missions such as Kepler, TESS, and Gaia, we have a wealth of data on pulsating white dwarfs that can be leveraged in white dwarf asteroseismology. We address the question of the proportion of white dwarfs with thin hydrogen layers versus those with thick hydrogen layers. We also provide a mass-radius relation for carbon-oxygen core, hydrogen atmosphere white dwarfs. Such a relationship can be used in conjunction with magnitudes and distance measurements to constrain the mass and effective temperature of the white dwarfs. We select eight hydrogen atmosphere, pulsating white dwarfs (DAVs), for their rich pulsation spectra. From such pulsation spectra, we can derive an asymptotic period spacing, which in turn allows us to determine the thickness of the hydrogen and helium envelope of the models, without having to perform period by period fitting. We find that the majority of the white dwarfs have thicker hydrogen layers and determine an upper limit of Mr = 1 - 10 to the -2.2 for the location of the base of the helium layer, in accordance with stellar evolution models. We confirm a finding from earlier studies that used a mass-radius relation and Gaia data to determine the effective temperatures of white dwarfs. The Gaia data systematically points to white dwarfs of lower effective temperature than indicated by the spectroscopy. Our results also support the hypothesis that white dwarfs with thicker hydrogen layers are more common than those with thinner layers.

AI.tldr: This study uses asteroseismology of eight pulsating white dwarfs (DAVs) to determine hydrogen layer thickness, derive a mass-radius relation, and find that most white dwarfs have thicker hydrogen layers, with Gaia data showing systematically lower effective temperatures than spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: To determine the proportion of white dwarfs with thin vs. thick hydrogen layers and to provide a mass-radius relation for carbon-oxygen core, hydrogen atmosphere white dwarfs using data from Kepler, TESS, and Gaia.
AI.method: Select eight hydrogen atmosphere pulsating white dwarfs (DAVs) with rich pulsation spectra; derive asymptotic period spacing from pulsation spectra to determine hydrogen and helium envelope thickness without period-by-period fitting; compare with Gaia data and mass-radius relations.
AI.result: Majority of white dwarfs have thicker hydrogen layers; determined upper limit of M_r = 1×10^{-2.2} for the base of the helium layer; Gaia data systematically indicates lower effective temperatures than spectroscopy; confirmed that white dwarfs with thicker hydrogen layers are more common.
AI.conclusion: Thicker hydrogen layers are more common among white dwarfs, consistent with stellar evolution models; Gaia data shows systematic offsets in temperature determination compared to spectroscopy; derived mass-radius relation can constrain mass and effective temperature when combined with magnitudes and distance measurements.

title: The Twentieth Data Release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey: First All-Sky BOSS Spectra, eROSITA-SDSS-V Mapper Coordinated Observations, and a Preview of the Local Volume Mapper
summary: This paper presents the twentieth data release (DR20) from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, the third data release of its fifth generation (SDSS-V). SDSS-V is a panoptic spectroscopy survey that is mapping the stars, gas, and galaxies through three scientific programs: the Milky Way Mapper (MWM), the Local Volume Mapper (LVM), and the Black Hole Mapper (BHM). DR20 presents the first optical (BOSS) SDSS-V spectra from southern hemisphere for the MWM and BHM surveys; new optical MWM and BHM data from the northern hemisphere are also available, for a total over 3 million spectra of 1.5 million stars and half a million galaxies and quasars, with galactic and extragalactic x-ray targets coordinate with eROSITA DR2. DR20 includes integral field spectroscopy maps from LVM of six targets and 169 tiles, spanning Galactic HII regions, planetary nebulae, and nearby galaxies. Additionally, eighteen value added catalogs are also released with DR20, based on SDSS-V MWM and BHM data, and we present a new LVM visualization tool including an RGB HiPS map as a value added product.

AI.tldr: SDSS-V DR20 releases over 3 million spectra from southern and northern hemispheres across three surveys (MWM, BHM, LVM), including first southern BOSS spectra, LVM integral field maps of 6 targets/169 tiles, and 18 value-added catalogs with a new visualization tool.
AI.motivation: To provide the astronomical community with the twentieth data release from SDSS, advancing panoptic spectroscopic mapping of stars, gas, and galaxies across the Milky Way and beyond.
AI.method: SDSS-V operates three scientific programs: Milky Way Mapper (MWM), Black Hole Mapper (BHM) using BOSS spectrographs, and Local Volume Mapper (LVM) using integral field spectroscopy. Data includes optical spectra from both hemispheres and LVM IFU maps.
AI.result: Over 3 million spectra covering 1.5 million stars and half a million galaxies/quasars; first southern hemisphere BOSS data; LVM maps of 6 targets across 169 tiles; 18 value-added catalogs; new RGB HiPS visualization tool for LVM.
AI.conclusion: DR20 significantly expands SDSS-V's sky coverage into the southern hemisphere and provides rich multi-survey spectroscopic data products with enhanced visualization capabilities for the community.

title: Ultracool and Brown Dwarf Candidates Identified via CatWISE-2MASS-Gaia DR3
summary: Ultracool and brown dwarf candidates ($d_{\odot}\lesssim 125$ pc, $|b|>8^{\circ}$) were identified via multiband and astrometric data from CatWISE ($W_1W_2$), 2MASS ($JHK_s$), and Gaia DR3 ($G$, $G_{RP}$, $π$, $μ_α$, $μ_δ$). $N\approx 11.8 \times 10^3$ candidates emerged once simultaneously constrained by color and absolute magnitude criteria (e.g., $G-W_2 \ge 1.75(G-J)-2.25$), whereby $\simeq 350$ sources are absent from the Gaia Ultracool Dwarf (UCD) catalog. Spectral types were approximated using a hybrid $M_G-M_{W_1}$ sigmoid that offers additional temperature coverage in certain cases. Subsequent efforts may focus on extending sampling to the deeper NIR VVVX footprint that partly encompasses the Galactic plane, and over the long-term spectroscopically (in)validating candidates missing from the Gaia UCD database.

AI.tldr: Using multiband and astrometric data from CatWISE, 2MASS, and Gaia DR3, about 11,800 ultracool and brown dwarf candidates were identified within ~125 pc, with ~350 not in the Gaia UCD catalog. Spectral types were approximated via a hybrid M_G-M_W1 sigmoid. Future work includes extending to deeper NIR VVVX data and spectroscopic validation.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize ultracool and brown dwarf candidates in the solar neighborhood (~125 pc) that are missing from existing catalogs, leveraging combined photometric and astrometric constraints.
AI.method: Multi-criteria selection using CatWISE (W1W2), 2MASS (JHKs), and Gaia DR3 (G, GRP, parallax, proper motions) with color and absolute magnitude cuts (e.g., G-W2 ≥ 1.75(G-J)-2.25). Spectral type approximation via a hybrid M_G-M_W1 sigmoid function.
AI.result: Identified ~11,800 candidates within 125 pc at |b|>8°, of which ~350 are absent from the Gaia UCD catalog. The hybrid sigmoid provides extended temperature coverage.
AI.conclusion: The work expands the known sample of nearby ultracool and brown dwarf candidates, with plans to extend to the VVVX Galactic plane footprint and to spectroscopically validate those missing from existing catalogs.

title: Stellar Population Astrophysics (SPA) with the TNG. Beyond the iron peak: Galactic evolution of molybdenum, ruthenium and zirconium through open clusters
summary:
Context: Open clusters serve as key laboratories for studying the chemical evolution of the Milky Way. In particular, leveraging these coeval groups of stars to study elements beyond the iron peak provides insights into heavy-element nucleosynthesis, whose origins remain uncertain.
  Aims: This work aims to determine the Mo, Ru, and Zr abundances for 81 stars across 30 open clusters. We compare these new chemical patterns with those of key reference elements (Y, Sr, Eu), which were previously derived by our group. This comparison seeks to disentangle the distinct contributions from various nucleosynthetic processes.
  Methods: Using the high-resolution spectra acquired within the Stellar Population Astrophysics programme using the HARPS-N echelle spectrograph at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo, we estimate chemical abundances through spectral synthesis with TSFitPy under local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) conditions.
  Results: This study provides the first Ru abundances for a large open cluster sample, alongside new measurements for Mo and Zr. We observe tight correlations between Mo, Ru, and other s-process elements (Sr, Y, Zr), with slopes near unity, suggesting common enrichment timescales. Conversely, relations with the r-process element Eu show significant deviations, implying additional nucleosynthetic contributions. Crucially, chemical planes involving [Mo/Ru] and [s/Mo] ratios suggest systematic offsets when compared to theoretical s-process predictions.

AI.tldr: This study presents the first large-sample Ru abundances (plus Mo, Zr) for 81 stars across 30 open clusters, revealing tight correlations with s-process elements (Sr, Y, Zr) but deviations from r-process element Eu, and systematic offsets from theoretical s-process predictions in chemical planes.
AI.motivation: Open clusters are key laboratories for studying Milky Way chemical evolution, and measuring heavy elements beyond the iron peak (Mo, Ru, Zr) helps disentangle contributions from different nucleosynthetic processes whose origins remain uncertain.
AI.method: High-resolution HARPS-N spectra from the Stellar Population Astrophysics programme were used. Chemical abundances were estimated via spectral synthesis with TSFitPy under local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) conditions.
AI.result: First Ru abundances for a large open cluster sample were obtained. Mo, Ru correlate tightly with s-process elements (Sr, Y, Zr) with slopes near unity, indicating common enrichment timescales. Relations with r-process element Eu show significant deviations. Chemical planes involving [Mo/Ru] and [s/Mo] ratios show systematic offsets from theoretical s-process predictions.
AI.conclusion: The correlations suggest common enrichment timescales for Mo, Ru, and other s-process elements, while deviations from Eu indicate additional nucleosynthetic contributions. Systematically offset chemical planes imply that current theoretical s-process predictions do not fully capture the observed abundance patterns.
